angle: Critiques, pitfalls, and reproducibility failures of ML applied to networking/security

papers.title: Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning in Computer Security
papers.authors: Daniel Arp, Erwin Quiring, Feargus Pendlebury, Alexander Warnecke, Fabio Pierazzi, Christian Wressnegger, Lorenzo Cavallaro, Konrad Rieck
papers.relevance: The canonical catalogue of ten pitfalls (sampling bias, label inaccuracy, data snooping, spurious correlations, inappropriate baselines/measures, base-rate fallacy, lab-only evaluation) shown to be widespread across 30 top-tier security-ML papers, and it explicitly recommends explanation techniques to surface spurious features, making it the methodological anchor for any XAI-for-traffic-classification critique.

papers.title: TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification across Space and Time
papers.authors: Feargus Pendlebury, Fabio Pierazzi, Roberto Jordaney, Johannes Kinder, Lorenzo Cavallaro
papers.relevance: Defines temporal and spatial experimental bias and shows published 0.99 F1 malware classifiers collapse under realistic time-aware splits, the template for auditing time-based data leakage in traffic-classification evaluations.

papers.title: TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification across Space and Time (Extended Version)
papers.authors: Zeliang Kan, Shae McFadden, Daniel Arp, Feargus Pendlebury, Roberto Jordaney, Johannes Kinder, Fabio Pierazzi, Lorenzo Cavallaro
papers.relevance: Updated TESSERACT with the AUT robustness metric and constraints for fair experiment design, extending the temporal/spatial-bias argument beyond Android malware.

papers.title: Troubleshooting an Intrusion Detection Dataset: the CICIDS2017 Case Study
papers.authors: Gints Engelen, Vera Rimmer, Wouter Joosen
papers.relevance: Documents label errors, CICFlowMeter implementation bugs (wrong TCP session termination, duplicated flows) and attack-simulation flaws in CIC-IDS2017, showing benchmark results on the uncorrected dataset are unreliable.

papers.title: Errors in the CICIDS2017 Dataset and the Significant Differences in Detection Performances It Makes
papers.authors: Maxime Lanvin, Pierre-Francois Gimenez, Yufei Han, Frederic Majorczyk, Ludovic Me, Eric Totel
papers.relevance: Independently finds further CICIDS2017 errors (mislabeled port-scan and botnet flows, duplicated packets) and quantifies how much detection scores change once labels are fixed - direct evidence that reported NIDS accuracy tracks dataset defects.

papers.title: Bad Design Smells in Benchmark NIDS Datasets
papers.authors: Robert Flood, Gints Engelen, David Aspinall, Lieven Desmet
papers.relevance: Systematizes recurring generation-pipeline defects ('design smells') across benchmark NIDS datasets - trivially predictive single features, tooling artifacts, unrealistic attack mixes - unifying the CICIDS-style error reports into a general critique.

papers.title: Establishing the Contaminating Effect of Metadata Feature Inclusion in Machine-Learned Network Intrusion Detection Models
papers.authors: Laurens D'hooge, Miel Verkerken, Bruno Volckaert, Tim Wauters, Filip De Turck
papers.relevance: Shows that metadata features (IPs, ports, timestamps) act as label proxies in CIC and other benchmark datasets, inflating scores - a concrete, named instance of classifiers keying on dataset artifacts rather than attack behavior.

papers.title: Discovering Non-Metadata Contaminant Features in Intrusion Detection Datasets
papers.authors: Laurens D'hooge, Miel Verkerken, Tim Wauters, Bruno Volckaert, Filip De Turck
papers.relevance: Follow-up showing contamination is not limited to obvious metadata: derived flow features (e.g., TTL-related and size statistics) also leak labels in benchmark IDS datasets, so simple feature-dropping does not fix shortcut learning.

papers.title: AI/ML for Network Security: The Emperor has no Clothes
papers.authors: Arthur S. Jacobs, Roman Beltiukov, Walter Willinger, Ronaldo A. Ferreira, Arpit Gupta, Lisandro Z. Granville
papers.relevance: Introduces TRUSTEE, which distills black-box traffic/security models into high-fidelity decision trees and uses those explanations to expose shortcut learning, spurious correlations and o.o.d. fragility in published models - the single closest bridge between XAI methods and the pitfalls literature for traffic classification.

papers.title: The Sweet Danger of Sugar: Debunking Representation Learning for Encrypted Traffic Classification
papers.authors: Yuqi Zhao, Giovanni Dettori, Matteo Boffa, Luca Vassio, Marco Mellia
papers.relevance: Critically re-assesses BERT-style traffic representation models (up to 98% claimed accuracy) and shows the successes stem from data-preparation shortcuts - spurious feature-label correlations that vanish in realistic settings - an 'are we there yet' style debunking of encrypted traffic classification.

papers.title: Bias in the Shadows: Explore Shortcuts in Encrypted Network Traffic Classification
papers.authors: Chuyi Wang, Xiaohui Xie, Tongze Wang, Yong Cui
papers.relevance: BiasSeeker, a model-agnostic statistical framework that detects dataset-specific shortcut features in raw-byte encrypted traffic across 19 public datasets, explicitly motivated by the inadequacy of model-specific interpretation techniques for shortcut detection.

papers.title: One Task to Rule Them All: A Closer Look at Traffic Classification Generalizability
papers.authors: Elham Akbari, Zihao Zhou, Mohammad A. Salahuddin, Noura Limam, Raouf Boutaba, et al.
papers.relevance: Shows state-of-the-art traffic classifiers overperform only in their original evaluation context: dataset-specific and model-specific properties fail to transfer when datasets, labels, or tasks change - a direct generalizability critique of the TC literature.

papers.title: Replication: Contrastive Learning and Data Augmentation in Traffic Classification Using a Flowpic Input Representation
papers.authors: Alessandro Finamore, Chao Wang, Jonatan Krolikowski, Jose M. Navarro, Fuxing Chen, Dario Rossi
papers.relevance: The flagship reproducibility study in deep-learning traffic classification: reproducing an IMC'22 flowpic paper on UCDAVIS19/ISCX-VPN/ISCX-Tor plus three more datasets, it uncovers a data-shift/leakage problem in the original and notes most TC literature ships no code artifacts.

papers.title: SoK: Pragmatic Assessment of Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Giovanni Apruzzese, Pavel Laskov, Johannes Schneider
papers.relevance: Argues research evaluations are too narrow to estimate the operational value of ML-NIDS (hardware, preprocessing, and deployment factors neglected) and proposes 'pragmatic assessment', validated with practitioner surveys.

papers.title: The Cross-evaluation of Machine Learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems
papers.authors: Giovanni Apruzzese, Luca Pajola, Mauro Conti
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
papers.relevance: First formal model (XeNIDS) for cross-dataset evaluation of ML-NIDS, exposing why papers that reuse the same outdated datasets as isolated testbeds overstate reliability and hide generalization failures.

papers.title: Outside the Closed World: On Using Machine Learning for Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Robin Sommer, Vern Paxson
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2010
papers.relevance: The seminal critique of why ML succeeds elsewhere but rarely in operational network intrusion detection: semantic gap, high cost of errors, traffic diversity, and lack of public training data - the intellectual ancestor of the whole pitfalls literature.

papers.title: Testing Intrusion Detection Systems: A Critique of the 1998 and 1999 DARPA Intrusion Detection System Evaluations as Performed by Lincoln Laboratory
papers.authors: John McHugh
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Information and System Security (TISSEC)
papers.relevance: The original benchmark-dataset critique: methodological flaws in the DARPA/KDD lineage (synthetic traffic realism, attack taxonomy, scoring) that still propagate into every KDD99/NSL-KDD-based traffic-classification result.

papers.title: An Analysis of the 1999 DARPA/Lincoln Laboratory Evaluation Data for Network Anomaly Detection
papers.authors: Matthew V. Mahoney, Philip K. Chan
papers.relevance: Classic demonstration of simulation artifacts: anomaly detectors on DARPA'99 keyed on idiosyncratic TTL values, client addresses and other regularities absent in real traffic - the archetype of the spurious-correlation findings now rediscovered in CIC datasets.

papers.title: Benchmarking the Benchmark -- Analysis of Synthetic NIDS Datasets
papers.authors: Siamak Layeghy, Marcus Gallagher, Marius Portmann
papers.venue: arXiv preprint / Journal of Information Security and Applications
papers.relevance: Statistically compares benign traffic in synthetic NIDS benchmarks (CIC/UNSW lineage) against two real-world networks and finds significant distributional divergence, undermining the external validity of results trained on synthetic testbeds.

papers.title: Machine Learning (In) Security: A Stream of Problems
papers.authors: Fabricio Ceschin, Marcus Botacin, Albert Bifet, Bernhard Pfahringer, Luiz S. Oliveira, Heitor M. Gomes, Andre Gregio
papers.venue: ACM Digital Threats: Research and Practice (DTRAP)
papers.relevance: Surveys the correct application of stream/online ML in security, cataloguing concept drift, concept evolution, delayed labels, class imbalance and adversarial drift as chronically mishandled issues in cybersecurity ML pipelines.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Generalization Failure in Lightweight Intrusion Detection Models for IIoT Networks
papers.authors: MD Azizul Hakim, Md Shihab Uddin, Talha Ibne Anis
papers.relevance: Uses explainability analysis to show lightweight IIoT IDS models rely overwhelmingly on coarse port-category features (96-435x more frequent in source-domain attacks than in target domains), and that coarsening the feature relocates rather than removes the shortcut - XAI directly diagnosing a dataset artifact.

papers.title: Machine Learning in Network Intrusion Detection: A Cross-Dataset Generalization Study
papers.authors: Marco Cantone, Claudio Marrocco, Alessandro Bria
papers.relevance: Large controlled study showing ML-NIDS performance collapses when train and test come from different datasets even with harmonized NetFlow features, quantifying the generalization gap the single-dataset literature hides.

papers.title: Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Robert Geirhos, Joern-Henrik Jacobsen, Claudio Michaelis, Richard Zemel, Wieland Brendel, Matthias Bethge, Felix A. Wichmann
papers.relevance: The concept paper that names and frames 'shortcut learning' (decision rules that pass benchmarks but fail o.o.d.) and recommends interpretation plus o.o.d. testing - the theoretical vocabulary the traffic-classification critique papers all borrow.

papers.title: SoK: Explainable Machine Learning for Computer Security Applications
papers.authors: Azqa Nadeem, Daniel Vos, Clinton Cao, Luca Pajola, Simon Dieck, Robert Baumgartner, Sicco Verwer
papers.relevance: Systematizes 300 XAI-for-security papers and identifies pitfalls in how explanations are developed and evaluated (e.g., explanations rarely validated with users or ground truth), framing model debugging as the most mature XAI use-case - the XAI-side complement to the dataset-pitfall literature.

papers.title: SoK: Explainable Machine Learning in Adversarial Environments
papers.authors: Maximilian Noppel, Christian Wressnegger
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2024
papers.relevance: Systematizes attacks on explanation methods and their security implications, cautioning that the XAI techniques used to audit traffic classifiers are themselves manipulable - a second-order pitfall for XAI-based NIDS auditing.

papers.title: In Search of netUnicorn: A Data-Collection Platform to Develop Generalizable ML Models for Network Security Problems
papers.authors: Roman Beltiukov, Wenbo Guo, Arpit Gupta, Walter Willinger
papers.relevance: The constructive follow-up to TRUSTEE: a closed-loop data-collection platform for iteratively removing the inductive biases (shortcuts, o.o.d. fragility) that explanation-based audits reveal in network-security models.

papers.title: Inter-dataset generalization strength of supervised machine learning methods for intrusion detection
papers.authors: Laurens D'hooge, Tim Wauters, Bruno Volckaert, Filip De Turck
papers.venue: Journal of Information Security and Applications
papers.relevance: Early systematic evidence that models trained on one CIC-family dataset barely transfer to sibling datasets, foreshadowing the contamination results and challenging claimed generality of ML-IDS.

papers.title: Towards a Standard Feature Set for Network Intrusion Detection System Datasets
papers.authors: Mohanad Sarhan, Siamak Layeghy, Marius Portmann
papers.relevance: Diagnoses the incomparability of NIDS results caused by each dataset's proprietary feature set and proposes NetFlow-based standard features (NF-CICIDS2017 etc.) to make cross-dataset evaluation possible at all.

papers.title: Evaluating Standard Feature Sets Towards Increased Generalisability and Explainability of ML-based Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Mohanad Sarhan, Siamak Layeghy, Marius Portmann
papers.relevance: Evaluates NetFlow vs CICFlowMeter feature sets across CSE-CIC-IDS2018, BoT-IoT and ToN-IoT and uses SHAP to compare which features drive detection, tying feature-set choice to both generalization and explainability.

papers.title: MAWIFlow Benchmark: Realistic Flow-Based Evaluation for Network Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Joshua Schraven, Alexander Windmann, Oliver Niggemann
papers.relevance: Builds a benchmark from real backbone traffic (MAWILab 2011/2016/2021) specifically because synthetic benchmarks 'fail to reflect statistical variability and temporal drift', and shows tree ensembles degrade sharply across years.

papers.title: AnoShift: A Distribution Shift Benchmark for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
papers.authors: Marius Dragoi, Elena Burceanu, Emanuela Haller, Andrei Manolache, Florin Brad
papers.relevance: Introduces IID/NEAR/FAR temporal splits on ten years of Kyoto-2006+ network traffic and shows anomaly detectors' performance decays with distribution shift, giving the traffic domain its own concept-drift benchmark.

papers.title: Measuring the Complexity of Benchmark NIDS Datasets via Spectral Analysis
papers.authors: Robert Flood, David Aspinall
papers.relevance: Quantifies how 'easy' benchmark NIDS datasets are via spectral complexity measures, explaining why near-perfect scores are achievable and providing a tool to rank dataset difficulty before trusting reported accuracy.

papers.title: Traffic Generation using Containerization for Machine Learning
papers.authors: Henry Clausen, Robert Flood, David Aspinall
papers.relevance: Diagnoses why lab-generated IDS datasets lack heterogeneity, ground-truth labels, scale and contemporary content, and proposes container-based generation with per-process ground truth as the remedy.

papers.title: Towards Reproducible Network Traffic Analysis
papers.authors: Jordan Holland, Paul Schmitt, Prateek Mittal, Nick Feamster
papers.relevance: Documents the lack of standardization in traffic-analysis pipelines (representations, splits, tooling) that produces incomparable results, and builds a standard-pipeline framework to enable reproduction.

papers.title: Lost in Translation: Intrusion Detection Research with 'Kaggle Datasets'
papers.authors: Jukka Ruohonen
papers.relevance: Critiques the secondary-distribution problem: IDS papers increasingly train on re-hosted 'Kaggle' copies of benchmark datasets with undocumented provenance and modifications, compounding label-error and reproducibility issues.

papers.title: AC-DC: Adaptive Ensemble Classification for Network Traffic Identification
papers.authors: Xi Jiang, Shinan Liu, Saloua Naama, Francesco Bronzino, Paul Schmitt, Nick Feamster
papers.relevance: Jiang et al.'s critique-flavored work arguing raw-traffic DL classifiers are too costly and fragile for modern operational settings (companion IETF talk: 'Towards Designing Robust and Efficient Classifiers for Encrypted Traffic in the Modern Internet'); NOTE: an exact 'Jiang et al. reproducibility of DL traffic classification' paper could not be located in arXiv/DBLP/Crossref/S2 - see notes.

papers.title: A Survey of Network-based Intrusion Detection Data Sets
papers.authors: Markus Ring, Sarah Wunderlich, Deniz Scheuring, Dieter Landes, Andreas Hotho
papers.relevance: The reference catalogue of 30+ NIDS datasets with 15 quality properties; its documented gaps (no perfect dataset, poor labeling, staleness) are the raw material every critique paper builds on.

papers.title: Deep Learning and Zero-Day Traffic Classification: Lessons Learned From a Commercial-Grade Dataset with Hundreds of Encrypted and Zero-Day Applications
papers.authors: Lixuan Yang, Alessandro Finamore, Feng Jun, Dario Rossi
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management
papers.relevance: Shows how conclusions drawn on small academic TC datasets change on a commercial-grade dataset with hundreds of apps and zero-day traffic, evidencing the academic-vs-operational gap the critique papers allege.

papers.title: DataZoo: Streamlining Traffic Classification Experiments
papers.authors: Jan Luxemburk, Karel Hynek
papers.relevance: Toolset standardizing dataset access, splits and metrics for traffic classification, created explicitly because ad-hoc dataset handling and undisclosed splits cause overly optimistic, irreproducible TC results.

papers.title: Open-Source Framework for Encrypted Internet and Malicious Traffic Classification
papers.authors: Ofek Bader, Adi Lichy, Amit Dvir, Ran Dubin, Chen Hajaj
papers.relevance: An open-source unified pipeline (OSF-EIMTC) for encrypted/malicious traffic classification intended to make feature extraction and model evaluation reproducible across studies.

papers.title: Navigating Shortcuts, Spurious Correlations, and Confounders: From Origins via Detection to Mitigation
papers.authors: David Steinmann, Felix Divo, Maurice Kraus, Antonia Wuest, Lukas Struppek, et al.
papers.relevance: Cross-domain survey unifying definitions, detection methods (including XAI-based detection) and mitigations for shortcut learning and spurious correlations - useful taxonomy for transferring shortcut-detection methodology into traffic classification.

notes: MUST-FINDS: located all except a literal 'Jiang et al. reproducibility of deep-learning traffic classification' paper, which does not appear to exist under that authorship: DBLP full-text query 'reproducibility traffic classification' returns 0 hits, Xi Jiang's complete arXiv cs.NI record contains no reproducibility paper, and S2/Crossref/WebSearch turned up nothing. The real reproducibility literature is Finamore et al. (IMC'23 Replication, which found data leakage in the IMC'22 flowpic paper), Holland et al. 2203.12410, DataZoo, and OSF-EIMTC; the closest Jiang-authored critique is AC-DC / the IETF MTEN talk 'Towards Designing Robust and Efficient Classifiers for Encrypted Traffic in the Modern Internet' (included, flagged). 'Are we there yet'-style ETC critiques are covered by 'The Sweet Danger of Sugar' (debunks 98%-accuracy representation-learning claims as data-preparation shortcuts) and 'One Task to Rule Them All' (generalizability collapse across contexts). ISCX VPN-nonVPN critique content retrieved via WebSearch: ~65% of VPN biflows are BlueStacks emulator traffic that should be filtered; VPN pcaps contain multiple connections where only client-VPN-server tunnels should exist; unencrypted HTML payloads found inside 'VPN' captures; per-app captures use distinct IPs making classification trivially shortcut-able (these findings appear in Sweet Danger of Sugar and Bias in the Shadows audits). RECURRING DATASETS under critique: CIC-IDS2017/CSE-CIC-IDS2018 (label errors, CICFlowMeter TCP-termination bugs, duplicated flows - Engelen 204c, Lanvin 49c), ISCX-VPN-nonVPN-2016 and ISCX-Tor (contamination, staleness, per-app IP shortcuts), DARPA98/99 + KDD99/NSL-KDD (simulation artifacts incl. TTL - McHugh, Mahoney&Chan), UNSW-NB15, BoT-IoT, ToN-IoT (feature-set incomparability - Sarhan), UCDAVIS19/MIRAGE19/MIRAGE22/UTMOBILENET (Finamore replication), Kyoto-2006+ (AnoShift drift), MAWILab (MAWIFlow), CTU-13. RECURRING MODELS: Random Forest/decision trees/XGBoost dominate flow-feature NIDS; 1D-CNNs on packet bytes (DeepPacket, FlowPic); CNN-BiLSTM; BERT-style pre-trained transformers on raw bytes (ET-BERT, YaTC-class models - the target of Sweet Danger and Bias in the Shadows); autoencoders for anomaly detection. RECURRING EXPLANATION METHODS in this sub-literature: decision-tree distillation (TRUSTEE), SHAP feature attribution (Sarhan, IIoT cross-domain study), statistical correlation auditing of raw bytes (BiasSeeker, model-agnostic by design because 'existing solutions heavily rely on model-specific interpretation techniques, which lack adaptability and generality'), permutation/feature importance for contaminant discovery (D'hooge). AUTHOR-STATED LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK (quotes where available): Arp et al.: pitfalls are 'widespread in the current security literature... with permeating impact on experimental results' - they call for explanation methods and better dataset documentation but note no automated pitfall detection exists. TESSERACT: constraints require large timestamped datasets; tuning algorithm needs labeled future data; scope limited to Android malware - explicitly invites replication in other security domains (done for NIDS by Apruzzese, MAWIFlow, AnoShift). Engelen et al.: corrected CICIDS2017 still inherits the testbed's design; they note remaining 'meaningless artifacts' and urge tool-level validation (taken up by Flood et al. 'Bad Design Smells', who find single-feature separability and generation-tool artifacts recur across benchmarks and call for dataset documentation standards). Lanvin et al.: fixes cover only identified error classes; 'significant differences in detection performances' imply prior comparisons are unsafe. D'hooge: even after dropping metadata, 'non-metadata contaminant features' persist - open problem of constructing uncontaminated features. Jacobs et al. (TRUSTEE): decision-tree explanations 'do not explain the root cause' of underspecification and require domain experts to interpret; future work = closing the loop from explanation to data collection (answered by netUnicorn, whose own stated limitation is that experiment-based collection cannot cover all deployment environments). Sweet Danger of Sugar: their fix, Pcap-Encoder, has 'complexity [that] questions its applicability in practical settings'; findings 'reveal flaws in dataset preparation' and demand 'a critical reassessment of the whole area'. Bias in the Shadows (BiasSeeker): semi-automated - category-specific validation still needs human review; shortcut taxonomy may be incomplete across unseen NTC tasks. One Task to Rule Them All: overperformance is 'dataset-specific and model-specific'; calls for multi-dataset, multi-task evaluation as the norm. Finamore et al.: 'the vast majority of TC literature lacks code artifacts, performance assessments across datasets and reference comparisons against ML methods'; they could reproduce most results but discovered a data-shift issue in UCDAVIS19 affecting the original conclusions. Apruzzese SoK: 'the state-of-research hardly allows one to estimate the value of ML for NID' - hardware and operational costs are unreported; pragmatic assessment checklist proposed. Sommer & Paxson: the 'semantic gap' and absence of public real-world data remain unsolved (echoed 15 years later by Layeghy's finding that synthetic benchmark traffic diverges statistically from real networks, and by MAWIFlow: 'benchmark datasets... rely on synthetically generated traffic, which fails to reflect the statistical variability and temporal drift encountered in operational environments'). Ceschin et al.: delayed labels and concept evolution have no accepted evaluation protocol in security. Cantone et al.: harmonized features alone do not fix cross-dataset transfer - cause attribution (covariate vs label shift) left open. Hakim et al.: 'coarsening port resolution relocates rather than removes a documented shortcut' and 'the evaluation protocol used can reverse which target network appears to pose the greater generalization' risk. Nadeem SoK: XAI-for-security evaluations rarely involve end users or ground-truth explanations; Noppel & Wressnegger: explanation methods are themselves attackable, so XAI-based audits need robustness analysis. GAP SYNTHESIS for XAI-NTC: (1) no automated, model-agnostic shortcut detector is validated across NTC tasks (BiasSeeker is first, 2026, semi-automated); (2) explanation-driven dataset repair loop (TRUSTEE->netUnicorn) has not been applied to encrypted traffic classification specifically; (3) no reproducibility study exists for XAI methods themselves in NTC (explanation stability across retraining/datasets); (4) temporal-bias-aware evaluation (TESSERACT-style) is absent from the ETC/pre-trained-model literature.
